content: Interleukin-5 (IL-5) is a key cytokine responsible for the proliferation, maturation, activation, and survival of eosinophils, which are immune cells that play a central role in airway inflammation and are a hallmark of asthma. Monoclonal antibodies targeting IL-5 or its receptor (IL-5Rα) have been shown to reduce asthma exacerbations, improve health-related quality of life (HRQoL), and enhance lung function in selected patients, particularly those with severe eosinophilic asthma. These findings have led to their inclusion in current asthma management guidelines. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of anti-IL-5 and anti-IL-5Rα therapies compared to placebo in reducing asthma exacerbations, improving HRQoL, and enhancing lung function in adults and children with chronic asthma, with a specific focus on those with eosinophilic asthma that is refractory to standard treatments. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared mepolizumab, reslizumab, and benralizumab to placebo in patients with asthma. A total of 17 studies involving approximately 7,600 participants met the inclusion criteria. Six studies evaluated mepolizumab, five assessed reslizumab, and six investigated benralizumab. One benralizumab study was terminated early and did not contribute data. Most studies focused on patients with severe eosinophilic asthma, although the definition of this condition varied slightly between studies. Only one study included children aged 6 to 17 years, while nine others included children over 12 years but did not report age-specific results. The overall risk of bias in the included studies was low, and the evidence was deemed to be of high certainty using the GRADE framework, except for intravenous (IV) mepolizumab and subcutaneous (SC) reslizumab, as these delivery routes are not currently licensed. Anti-IL-5 therapies significantly reduced the rate of clinically significant asthma exacerbations (defined as requiring systemic corticosteroids for three or more days) by approximately 50% in patients with severe eosinophilic asthma who were on standard care (at least medium-dose inhaled corticosteroids) but had poorly controlled disease (defined as two or more exacerbations in the previous year or an Asthma Control Questionnaire (ACQ) score of 1.5 or higher). The rate ratios for exacerbation reduction were as follows: Mepolizumab SC: 0.45 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.36 to 0.55; high-certainty evidence) Mepolizumab IV: 0.53 (95% CI 0.44 to 0.64; moderate-certainty evidence) Reslizumab IV: 0.43 (95% CI 0.33 to 0.55; high-certainty evidence) Benralizumab SC: 0.59 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.66; high-certainty evidence) In non-eosinophilic participants, benralizumab also reduced exacerbation rates significantly, an effect not observed with reslizumab IV. However, no data were available for non-eosinophilic participants treated with mepolizumab. All anti-IL-5 therapies improved HRQoL scores in patients with severe eosinophilic asthma. However, only benralizumab achieved the minimum clinically important difference (MCID) for the St George's Respiratory Questionnaire (SGRQ; a 4-point change). Improvements in the ACQ and Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire (AQLQ), which focus on asthma symptoms, did not meet the MCID (0.5-point change) for any of the interventions. Evidence for HRQoL improvements in non-eosinophilic participants treated with benralizumab and reslizumab was weak, and subgroup analyses did not show significant differences. Anti-IL-5 therapies produced modest improvements in pre-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) in eosinophilic participants, with mean increases ranging from 0.08 L to 0.15 L. These changes are unlikely to be perceptible to patients. No excess serious adverse events were reported with any anti-IL-5 therapy. In fact, benralizumab was associated with a reduction in serious adverse events, likely due to fewer asthma-related hospitalizations. There was no difference in adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation for mepolizumab or reslizumab compared to placebo. However, a slightly higher proportion of participants discontinued benralizumab due to adverse events compared to placebo (2.1% vs. 0.9%), although the absolute numbers were small. The clinical implications of this finding remain unclear. In conclusion, anti-IL-5 therapies are effective as an adjunct to standard care in patients with severe eosinophilic asthma and poor symptom control. These treatments approximately halve the rate of asthma exacerbations in this population. However, evidence for improvements in HRQoL and lung function is limited, and the observed changes may not reach clinically meaningful levels. No significant safety concerns were identified for mepolizumab or reslizumab, and benralizumab was associated with a reduction in serious adverse events, although the higher rate of treatment discontinuation warrants further investigation. Future research should focus on identifying biomarkers to predict treatment response, determining the optimal duration and long-term effects of therapy, assessing the risk of relapse upon treatment withdrawal, and evaluating the efficacy of these therapies in non-eosinophilic patients and children, particularly those under 12 years of age. Comparative studies between different anti-IL-5 therapies and other biologic treatments are also needed. For benralizumab, future studies should closely monitor adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation.
